docs.title: What Was Difficult?
docs.text: I wanted to reflect on the relatively poor performance I delivered. I've never really used Quickshell... well, I've used it but never wrote with it so everything was pretty foreign to me. First of all, I'm not at all good at coding but I sort of found out that Quickshell is really really easy.. doesn't mean I can make good stuff though.

docs.title: Annoying
docs.text:
Honestly, Quickshell is pretty cool but QML is.. well it's odd. I don't have quite enough experience to make a valid opinion on it but its a little weird. QML is weirdly forgiving, you can basically violate syntax and it just goes ¯\(ツ)/¯ and moves on. When this is paired with UI creation, it makes the stupidest things so difficult to debug. Also doesn't help that I'm not good at it. I probably can't express this with words very easily but QML (and Qt specifically) is something that you can get to work but bugs (not necessarily errors) are way easier to make and at some point, you make this disgusting web of UI components that make the code hard to read and hard to fix issues. Maybe this is just my problem idk (ᵕ—.—). Also, for some reason SystemClock just makes the bar vanish? Please debug this, me, but it doesn't kill Quickshell. The bar just vanishes.

[!NOTE] SystemClock thing Quick update, the issue was resolved by setting the precision to minutes? No idea why it would kill the bar on seconds but idk.. (¬_¬)

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text: As a sort of guide for me, what do I want to do next? Well I need to fix the bugs of course, the bar is ridden with those. Other than bugs, I would like to implement a sort of settings menu that changes basic stuff like font size and font family, as well as make it possible to easily configure widgets. The bar layout already makes this quite easy but I still need to figure out how I would do this.

docs.text:
• That settings launcher
    • Here's where QML kind of shines, it can parse data from JSON for example so I could just have a pragma Singleton type file with settings that takes info from the JSON. I'd create this data using the settings launcher thing, which uses TextField or similar to take input from users and give the JSON a default so QML doesn't read nothing.

Issue with this is that traditional workspace Repeater thing you see can't rely on this, which is fine. For other widgets like an audio visualizer, I would also need a custom widget.

docs.title: QML
docs.text: On the decision to use QML (or more specifically, Quickshell), what it does and how it works.

docs.title: Why?
docs.text: I chose QML because Quickshell uses it and I know how cool Quickshell can be. It's like the difference between choosing to build a PC or buy one prebuilt.. I guess one's preferences would influence that decision but I think it's more fun! <(￣︶￣)>

docs.title: What?
docs.text: ^1Quickshell is a 'toolkit' for building a desktop shell. It uses QtQuick configured with QML.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• 'Hot-reloading', allows you to make config changes and the shell adapts without reloading manually.
  • Wayland integration (the future of linux desktop)
  • MPRIS compatible (media control).
  • Greetd, a desktop manager. Will not be used in this project but I will come back to this later.

docs.title: Colors
docs.text: What colors am I using, where do they come from?

docs.title: Singleton
docs.text: Singletons in QML are limited to one per engine, they can integrate other languages and file formats (like json) to do stuff. The Colors.qml file is a singleton, it is created by (https://github.com/InioX/matugen)[matugen] (and its input is configured by me) and dicatates different colors used across the entire project. All these 'properties' can be referenced globally, makes it really easy to set colors.. and you'll be doing that a little bit for a rice.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text: How do I want to break down the layout of the bar?

docs.title: Modularity
docs.text: I can make the bar 'modular' by keeping sections separated (right, left, middle). Inside these sections will be the widgets.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text: Within sections I can hold widgets, I will create a generic item that can be used across widgets (because they will all look uniform). This item will hold variables which can be modified by the actual widget when it is called.

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
The bar exist in the top layer of Wayland. Under PanelWindow, you can simply put WlrLayershell.layer: WlrLayer.Top. This is recommended by the Quickshell docs as well, it lets the PanelWindow exist with or without Wayland. Well, kind of, but for all of this config, I will assume Wayland is used.

[!NOTE] Fact I should look into it but it seems that Wayland can tell if something is a 'bar', even if the layer is lesser than Top. Maybe this is determined by the anchors?

docs.title: Screens
docs.text: using Variants (with the Quickshell.screens model) under Scope, Quickshell applies all my bar configs to every screen. Basically a glorified for loop.

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
• QtQuick, QtQuick elements (universal)
  • Quickshell, Quickshell elements (universal)
  • QtQuick.Layouts, used for things like RowLayouts. Makes it easy to nest components. Also provides Qt.LeftToRight and Qt.RightToLeft, useful for the sections I will make in the bar.
  • Quickshell.Wayland, provides Wayland integration. Will be used mostly for layering as well as locking, backgrounds, idling maybe.
  • Quickshell.Hyprland, Hyprland integration. This gives Quickshell access to workspace IDs (for the workspace widget) and focusing.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
With imports in mind, I can narrow down code that would be used.

for every screen
Scope{
    Variants{
    model: Quickshell.screens, every screen, put modelData in Bar.qml file as requird property

    Bar, call the bar component


    }
}

create the bar,
PanelWindow{
    required property var modelData, for iteration across screens

    anchors

    implicitHeight

    WlrLayershell.layer: WlrLayer.Top (not needed but here for clarification)

    RowLayout{
        call each section

        Left

        Right

        Middle
    }
}

to hold widgets
RowLayout{
    anchor.left: parent.left, anchor to the left
    layoutDirection: Qt.RightToLeft 

    Widgets
}

```Widget.qml, the generic widget component that all widgets will use import like everyting in Quickshell basically

Rectangle{ id item

create variables to be used by widgets
property string icon: "", icons, if used
property string content: "", data

signal clicked()

RowLayout{

    display icon
    display text

    MouseArea{

        use clicked() function, send to item
    }
}

}

```

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
There are a few ways to parse audio given to me. One way is to take audio information from a terminal using a Process with a Timer (can I omit a timer and just have Process run when something about audio changes?). Another way is using Quickshell's built-in Pipewire service. This method makes it really easy, just define a PwNode property that references Pipewire's default node Something funny that I encountered is that if I set the volume to the vol property, which is a real, or a float (idk why it's named that way) to 0, it changes the text to just '0' which I don't want. I want floats in case I used percentages so I made a check to see if vol was \=== to ref (which is just a 0.00 real, not quite sure why I made it) and if it was, return "0.00", a string. Otherwise (if it is greater than ref), it returns the actual volume in a 2 decimal float. Kinda weird the way I did it but I thought it was a little funny.

[!NOTE] real vs. string The difference is obvious but here's an error I made, I was assigning the audio.volume of defNode to a real property. This kinda messed stuff up because that property called toFixed(2) which actually turns the returned value into a string already, so making it a real just messes things up (it wasn't returning 2 decimal places). Made it a string instead. This does mess up the check I made for vol, where if it's === to ref, it returns "OFF" so I just need to make another property.

docs.title: Mute Check
docs.text:
I decided to have the widget relay if Pipewire's default node was muted or not. This kind of taught me something interesting, QML doesn't really have ifs.. it does but not really. I could set the widget's text to mute ? "MUT":"VOL" which is literally just asking (before the text is sent) whether or not the bool 'mute' is true. After the ?, it's basically an array. If mute is true, 'MUT' is sent. If it isn't true, 'VOL' (the default) is sent. Interesting. Another thing I learned is that ! can flip a boolean, I can see this being used in many ways. Like (pseudocode)

//when onClicked function in MouseArea gets triggered, flip the mute bool
onClicked(): mute = !mute
